source_text: Docet non tantum contemnendas sed et periculosas esse diuitias, illic esse radicem malorum blandientium, caecitatem mentis humanae occulta deceptione fallentium. unde et diuitem stultum saeculares copias cogitantem et se exuberantium fructuum largitate iactantem redarguit Deus dicens: stulte, hac nocte expostulatur anima tua. quae ergo parasti cuius erunt? laetabatur stultus in fructibus nocte moriturus et cui uita iam deerat uictus abundantiam cogitabat. contra autem Dominus perfectum et consummatum docet fieri qui omnibus suis uenditis adque in usum pauperum distributis thesaurum sibi condat in caelo. eum dicit posse se sequi et gloriam dominicae passionis imitari qui expeditus et succinctus nullis laqueis rei familiaris inuoluitur, sed solutus ac liber facultates suas ad Dominum ante praemissas ipse quoque comitatur. ad quod ut possit unusquisque nostrum parare se, sic discit orare et de orationis lege qualis esse debeat noscere.
thought_title: Riches are dangerous; the free man follows Christ
orientation: Cyprian is explaining the petition for daily bread, and has just cited Paul on contentment; he now contrasts the rich fool with the one who sells all and follows Christ.
pass_a_gloss: He teaches that riches are not only to be despised but also dangerous, that there is the root of flattering evils, the blindness of the human mind deceiving by hidden deception. Therefore God also rebukes the rich fool thinking about worldly resources and boasting in the abundance of overflowing fruits, saying: Fool, this night your soul is demanded. Therefore the things you have prepared, whose will they be? The fool was rejoicing in fruits, about to die in the night, and he whose life was already failing was thinking about abundance of food. On the other hand, the Lord teaches that he becomes perfect and complete who, with all his things sold and distributed for the use of the poor, stores up treasure for himself in heaven. He says that he can follow him and imitate the glory of the Lord's passion who, unencumbered and girded, is entangled in no snares of household property, but released and free, with his resources sent ahead to the Lord, he himself also accompanies them. So that each one of us may be able to prepare himself for this, he thus learns to pray and to know from the law of prayer what kind of person he ought to be.

choices.why: Keeps the genitive plural 'malorum' as 'evils' and the participle 'blandientium' as 'flattering' to preserve the active, deceptive quality Cyprian attributes to riches.
rejected: root of all kinds of evil

choices.term: caecitatem mentis humanae occulta deceptione fallentium
choices.english: blindness of the human mind deceiving by hidden deception
choices.why: Preserves the double idea of hiddenness and deception in 'occulta deceptione' and keeps 'fallentium' as an active participle modifying the evils.
rejected: blindness of the human mind that deceives with hidden trickery

choices.why: Keeps the passive force of 'expostulatur' and the legal sense of a demand being made, matching the gospel wording.
rejected: your soul is required of you

choices.english: stores up treasure for himself in heaven
choices.why: Keeps the reflexive 'sibi' and the verb 'condat' as 'stores up' to preserve the image of laying away wealth.
rejected: lays up treasure for himself in heaven

choices.why: Preserves the two adjectives as a pair describing readiness for travel, matching the imagery of following Christ.

choices.term: facultates suas ad Dominum ante praemissas
choices.english: with his resources sent ahead to the Lord
choices.why: Keeps the ablative absolute structure and the idea of sending wealth ahead, which Cyprian uses to describe detachment.
rejected: having sent his possessions ahead to the Lord

bible_refs.note: stulte, hac nocte expostulatur anima tua. quae ergo parasti cuius erunt?

pass_b_english: He teaches that riches are not only to be despised but are also dangerous, that in them is the root of flattering evils, the blindness of the human mind, deceived by hidden deception. So God rebukes the foolish rich man who was thinking about his worldly resources and boasting of the abundance of his overflowing harvests: "Fool, this night your soul is demanded. What you have prepared, whose will it be?" (Luke 12:20). The fool was rejoicing in his harvests on the night he was about to die, and the man whose life was already slipping away was thinking about the abundance of his food. But the Lord teaches that the one who sells everything, distributes it for the use of the poor, and stores up treasure for himself in heaven becomes perfect and complete. He says that the one who is unencumbered and girded, entangled in no snares of household property, but free and unbound, with his resources sent ahead to the Lord, himself following after them, can follow him and imitate the glory of the Lord's passion. So that each of us may be able to prepare himself for this, he learns to pray in this way and to know from the law of prayer what he ought to be.

problems.quote: the blindness of the human mind deceiving by hidden deception
problems.source_quote: caecitatem mentis humanae occulta deceptione fallentium
problems.why: English makes mind the deceiver; Latin has riches/blinding evils deceiving the mind.
problems.fix: the blindness of the human mind, deceived by hidden deception
problems.ruling: 'fallentium' (genitive plural) modifies 'malorum'; riches/evils deceive the mind, not mind deceiving.

edits.old: the blindness of the human mind deceiving by hidden deception
edits.new: the blindness of the human mind, deceived by hidden deception

fixed: Agency: 'fallentium' modifies the evils/riches that deceive the mind, not the mind deceiving; changed to 'deceived by hidden deception'.

problems.quote: He says that the one who can follow him and imitate the glory of the Lord's passion is unencumbered and girded
problems.source_quote: eum dicit posse se sequi et gloriam dominicae passionis imitari qui expeditus et succinctus
problems.why: The unencumbered man is the one said to be able to follow and imitate; English reverses who is able and who is unencumbered.
problems.fix: He says that the one who is unencumbered and girded, caught in no snares of household property, but free and unbound, his resources sent ahead to the Lord and himself following them, can follow him and imitate the glory of the Lord's passion.
problems.ruling: "eum dicit posse se sequi... qui expeditus et succinctus": the unencumbered man is the one able to follow; English wrongly makes unencumbered the predicate of 'one who can follow'.

edits.old: He says that the one who can follow him and imitate the glory of the Lord's passion is unencumbered and girded, entangled in no snares of household property, but free and unbound, with his resources sent ahead to the Lord, and he himself follows after them.
edits.new: He says that the one who is unencumbered and girded, entangled in no snares of household property, but free and unbound, with his resources sent ahead to the Lord, himself following after them, can follow him and imitate the glory of the Lord's passion.

fixed: agency: real — source 'eum dicit posse se sequi et gloriam dominicae passionis imitari qui expeditus et succinctus' makes unencumbered/girded the identifying description and ability to follow/imitate the assertion, so reversed the English clauses.

last_rejected.quote: he learns to pray in this way
last_rejected.why: Subject is Christ (Dominus), not generic 'he'; English hides Christ as teacher.
last_rejected.fix: so that each of us may be able to prepare himself for this, Christ teaches us to pray in this way
last_rejected.ruling: 'Dominus' is the subject of 'docet' above; 'discit' continues it. 'He' naturally refers back to the Lord as teacher.

last_rejected.quote: the glory of the Lord's passion
last_rejected.why: 'dominicae' refers to Christ's own passion, not 'the Lord's passion' as separate from Christ.
last_rejected.ruling: 'dominicae passionis' = 'Lord's passion'; 'dominicae' is standard for Christ's. English 'Lord's passion' correctly conveys this.

last_rejected.quote: the root of flattering evils, the blindness of the human mind, deceived by hidden deception
last_rejected.source_quote: radicem malorum blandientium, caecitatem mentis humanae occulta deceptione fallentium
last_rejected.why: Both participles modify malorum; the evils deceive the mind's blindness. English makes blindness a second thing that merely exists, deceived.
last_rejected.fix: that in them is the root of flattering evils, which deceive the blindness of the human mind by a hidden deception.
last_rejected.ruling: Grammar is ambiguous: 'fallentium' may agree with 'malorum' (evils deceiving blindness) or stand in apposition; English 'deceived by hidden deception' is a defensible reading, not a clear meaning change.

last_rejected.quote: he learns to pray in this way and to know from the law of prayer what he ought to be.
last_rejected.source_quote: sic discit orare et de orationis lege qualis esse debeat noscere
last_rejected.why: Subject/agency muddled: 'he' is vague, and 'qualis esse debeat' refers to what the prayer ought to be like, not what the person ought to be.
last_rejected.fix: so he learns to pray in this way, and to know from the law of prayer what sort of prayer it ought to be.
last_rejected.ruling: Subject of discit and debeat is unusquisque; de orationis lege is the source, so qualis esse debeat rightly means what he ought to be.
